narrative:
Your application was reviewed carefully, and while we recognize your strong efforts and achievements, the decision was made to deny admission based on the likelihood of passing the bar exam on your first attempt. The model assessing your profile estimated a 51% chance of not passing the bar, which is just above the threshold where we can confidently offer admission. This prediction isn’t a reflection of your potential in the long term, but rather an assessment of how your current academic and situational factors compare to students who have historically succeeded in this specific challenge.

The most significant factor in this decision was your academic performance in your third year of law school, where your grades placed you in the lowest decile. This stood out because students who pass the bar on their first try typically rank much higher—around the sixth decile—by their final year. While your undergraduate GPA was actually above the average of students who passed the bar, and your LSAT score was close to the typical range, these strengths weren’t enough to offset the concern raised by your third-year performance. Additionally, the model noted that you plan to attend law school part-time, which is less common among students who pass the bar on their first attempt—only about 7% of them do so while balancing other commitments.

Your family’s lower-middle income bracket was also considered, as students from higher-income backgrounds tend to have slightly better pass rates, though this was a smaller factor in the decision. It’s important to note that this assessment doesn’t account for personal resilience, work ethic, or other qualities that aren’t captured in the data. If you choose to reapply, focusing on improving your academic standing in your final year of law school—particularly in courses that align with bar exam subjects—could significantly strengthen your profile. Alternatively, gaining more legal experience or retaking the LSAT to achieve a higher score might also help shift the prediction in your favor. This decision isn’t final, and with targeted effort, you can absolutely position yourself for success in the future.
